e: Private subnets need a NAT gateway placed in a public subnet to reach the internet. One NAT gateway per AZ, each with a route table in its own AZ, keeps it highly available and avoids cross-AZ dependency. NAT instances require management, a second internet gateway isn't allowed, and an egress-only gateway is for IPv6.

DataSync automates the transfer: an on-premises DataSync agent reads from the source file system, and a DataSync location configuration defines the source server and the EFS destination so tasks can run automatically. Manual copy commands and extra EBS volumes aren't needed, and AZ placement isn't required for the transfer.

AWS Glue job bookmarks keep state about data already processed, so each run handles only new data. Deleting data, changing workers, or using FindMatches (a deduplication ML transform) doesn't stop reprocessing.

Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS detection and mitigation (and DDoS response team support), and CloudFront absorbs and distributes attack traffic at the edge for both static and dynamic content. GuardDuty only detects, blocking thousands of IPs with network ACLs doesn't scale, and Spot Instances can be interrupted.

EventBridge must be allowed to invoke the function, which is done with a resource-based policy on the Lambda function that allows lambda:InvokeFunction for the events.amazonaws.com service principal. This is the least privilege. An execution role controls what the function can do, not who can invoke it, and lambda:* or '*' is too broad.

SSE-KMS logs key usage in CloudTrail for auditing, and KMS can automatically rotate customer managed keys every year, so it's the most operationally efficient. SSE-S3 doesn't provide per-use key logs, SSE-C leaves key management to the customer, and manual rotation is extra work.

API Gateway provides the REST API, and Lambda can write and read the location data to a datastore, which fits a multi-tier design with an API. Athena, QuickSight, and Kinesis Data Analytics are analytics tools and don't give a REST API for storing and retrieving data points.

RDS event notifications published to an SNS topic can fan out to multiple SQS queues, one per target system, so each target consumes the sale event independently, with Lambda updating the targets. Fan-out is SNS to SQS, not SQS to SNS, and a single queue can't deliver the same message to multiple targets.

S3 Object Lock with versioning and a legal hold keeps objects immutable with no fixed expiry until the hold is removed, and only users granted s3:PutObjectLegalHold can remove the hold and so delete the objects. A fixed 100-year retention doesn't match 'nonspecific time', and Glacier vault lock is for vaults, not S3 objects.

Presigned URLs let browsers upload directly to S3, taking upload load off the web servers, and S3 event notifications invoking Lambda resize images asynchronously, which decouples resizing from the upload. Uploading to Glacier, uploading through the web server, or scheduled resizing don't improve decoupling and speed.

Amazon MQ with an active/standby broker across AZs makes the broker highly available and managed, an Auto Scaling group of consumers across two AZs keeps the consumers available, and RDS Multi-AZ gives a managed highly available database. Self-managed replicas or a single extra consumer give less availability and more operational work.

Running the existing containers on ECS with Fargate needs no code changes and no server management, with Service Auto Scaling and an ALB to handle growth. Two EC2 instances don't scale or reduce operations, and rewriting for Lambda or using HPC means major development effort.

There's no spare network bandwidth for 50 TB, so a Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device moves the data offline quickly. The transformation job is then rebuilt in AWS with Glue, which is serverless and low in operational overhead. DataSync needs network bandwidth, and Snowcone is too small.

Lambda scales automatically with varying numbers of users to process photos, S3 stores the photo objects, and DynamoDB keeps the metadata. DynamoDB isn't meant for photo storage, Firehose isn't a processing and storage app solution, and adding fixed EC2 instances doesn't scale with variable demand.

Moving the instances to private subnets and adding an S3 gateway VPC endpoint linked to the private subnet route table gives a private route to S3 with no internet path. A NAT gateway still uses the internet, security groups don't change the path, and Direct Connect is unnecessary and costly.

A static website hosted on S3 needs no servers or patching and scales automatically, and CloudFront in front adds HTTPS, caching, and edge delivery for security and scale. WAF doesn't provide HTTPS, and Lambda or EC2 with ALB add operational work for content that isn't dynamic.

A CloudWatch Logs subscription can stream log data to OpenSearch Service in near real time as a built-in integration, with minimal setup. Custom Lambda functions, Firehose configurations, or agents on each server add more work or infrastructure to maintain.

Amazon S3 scales without limit and is the cheapest option for 900 TB of text documents with high demand. EBS has size limits and is tied to an AZ, EFS costs much more at this size, and OpenSearch is a search service, not a document repository.

AWS Firewall Manager lets you centrally configure and apply AWS WAF rules (blocking SQL injection and cross-site scripting) across multiple accounts and Regions, which is the least administrative effort. Setting up WAF separately in every account and Region is repetitive, and Shield focuses on DDoS rather than SQLi/XSS.

Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes traffic to the closest healthy endpoint, with endpoint groups in both Regions and the NLBs as endpoints, improving performance and availability for a DNS (UDP/TCP) service. CloudFront doesn't front a DNS service, and Route 53 alone doesn't give the same fast failover.

An existing unencrypted RDS instance can't be encrypted in place. Copy the latest snapshot with encryption enabled, then restore it as a new encrypted instance that replaces the old one. Encrypted instances automatically encrypt their snapshots and backups going forward.

AWS KMS is a managed service for creating, controlling, and auditing encryption keys at scale and integrates with AWS services and SDKs, which minimizes operational burden. MFA and IAM policies only protect access, and ACM manages TLS certificates, not data encryption keys.

Terminating SSL on an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener (using the certificate imported into ACM) offloads encryption and decryption from the web servers, freeing their CPU. Installing certificates on instances or a proxy EC2 instance doesn't remove the load, and S3 can't terminate SSL.

The job is stateless, interruptible, and can be restarted without harm, which fits Spot Instances well and gives the lowest cost at scale. Reserved or On-Demand Instances cost more, and Lambda has a 15-minute limit, so a 60+ minute job doesn't fit.

Launch the EC2 instances in private subnets with an Auto Scaling group and place the RDS Multi-AZ instance in private subnets so neither is exposed. Put the ALB in public subnets, and use NAT gateways in each AZ so private instances can reach the payment service while staying highly available. (In this PDF, option D's text is merged from two variants; the correct design has two public subnets, two private subnets, two NAT gateways, and the ALB in the public subnets.)
